results.result: The study employed a within-subjects design with 21 participants (after exclusions) undergoing two TMS-rsfMRI sessions targeting V1/V2 and FEF, with appropriate ethical approval and counterbalancing.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C11 provide a complete description of the experimental design, including sample size justification (C2), exclusion criteria (C3), counterbalancing (C11), and ethical procedures (C55-C56). The design is appropriate for the research question and follows established protocols.

results.result: At baseline, V1/V2 showed positive connectivity with visual network regions and anticorrelation with bilateral FEF, while FEF showed widespread connectivity with fronto-parietal networks and anticorrelation with default mode regions.
results.evaluation: Claims C12-C17 report baseline connectivity patterns with appropriate statistical thresholds (p<0.05 FWE) and are consistent with prior literature (C33-C34). The findings replicate known resting-state network organization and provide necessary baseline characterization for the intervention effects.

results.result: Inhibitory TMS of V1/V2 resulted in the emergence of positive correlations between V1/V2 and bilateral FEF, as well as increased connectivity with extrastriate and parietal visual areas.
results.evaluation: Claims C18-C19 report statistically significant changes (p<0.05 FWE) that were replicated with different ROI sizes (C92) and preprocessing approaches (C88). The emergence of positive V1/V2-FEF connectivity following V1/V2 inhibition represents a key experimental finding supported by appropriate statistical analyses.

results.result: Inhibitory TMS of FEF resulted in reduced positive correlations between FEF and bilateral visual areas including fusiform and occipital gyri.
results.evaluation: Claim C20 reports statistically significant reductions in connectivity (p<0.05 FWE) that contrast with the V1/V2 stimulation effects. The finding was replicated with different ROI sizes and preprocessing methods, demonstrating robustness of the opposite effects of stimulating different hierarchical levels.

results.result: TMS-induced changes in local BOLD signal amplitude (ALFF) at the stimulation site were significantly correlated with remote changes in functional connectivity, particularly for FEF (r=0.6, p<0.01).
results.evaluation: Claims C21-C22 report significant correlations between local signal changes and remote connectivity changes, with appropriate statistical tests. The correlation for V1/V2 was trend-level (p=0.05, C22), which is appropriately reported. Control analyses with contralateral regions showed no effects, supporting specificity.

results.result: DCM analysis revealed that V1/V2 stimulation altered feedforward connectivity to occipito-parietal cortex (p=0.04), while FEF stimulation decreased feedback connectivity to V1/V2 (p=0.0026 and p=0.0012).
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C25 report DCM results with appropriate statistical tests showing directional effects. The findings are consistent with the functional connectivity results and provide mechanistic insight into feedforward vs. feedback modulation. However, the p-value for V1/V2 feedforward effect (p=0.04) is marginal.

results.result: Computational modeling using the Kuramoto model reproduced the experimental findings, showing that simulated inhibition of V1/V2 increased connectivity with the rest of the brain while simulated inhibition of FEF decreased connectivity.
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C31 demonstrate that the computational model successfully reproduced the key experimental findings. The model was calibrated to baseline data (r=0.55 for V1/V2, r=0.45 for FEF, C128-C129) and showed consistent patterns with empirical results. Control simulations with other regions (C119-C121) support specificity.

results.result: The opposing effects of V1/V2 and FEF inhibition can be explained by an intrinsic hierarchical ordering of cortical timescales, where inhibition reduces synchronization discrepancy for V1/V2 but increases it for FEF.
results.evaluation: Claims C38, C41-C42, and C45 present the main theoretical interpretation supported by computational modeling (C27-C31) and consistent with cited literature on cortical timescale hierarchies. The mechanistic explanation is well-supported by both experimental and modeling results, though it remains a model-based inference rather than direct measurement.

results.result: TMS targets were individualized using neuronavigation, with continuous theta-burst stimulation (40s, 3 pulses at 50 Hz, 200ms intervals) delivered at 80% active motor threshold using validated protocols.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C69 provide comprehensive methodological details for TMS delivery with appropriate citations to established protocols (Huang et al., 2005). The individualization procedure (C59-C60) and intensity determination (C68-C69) follow standard practices. Methods are sufficiently detailed for replication.

results.result: Resting-state fMRI data were acquired using eyes-open protocol with fixation, monitored by eye-tracking, on a 3T Siemens Trio scanner with standard EPI parameters.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C76 describe appropriate rsfMRI acquisition methods. The eyes-open protocol choice is justified (C73) and monitored (C72). Scanner parameters (C75-C76) are standard for resting-state studies. The methodological choices are well-justified and adequately described.

results.result: fMRI preprocessing included standard steps (motion correction, coregistration, normalization, smoothing, bandpass filtering) with appropriate quality control showing no significant differences in motion between pre- and post-TMS scans.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C88 describe comprehensive preprocessing with appropriate quality control (C84-C85). The decision not to use global signal regression is justified (C86) and tested (C87-C88). Motion parameters were equivalent across conditions, supporting validity of the connectivity comparisons. Methods follow current best practices.

results.result: Seed-to-voxel connectivity analyses used 7.5mm radius ROIs centered on TMS targets, with results replicated using 10mm and 15mm ROIs, analyzed with appropriate statistical tests (FWE p<0.05).
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C96 describe appropriate connectivity analysis methods with proper statistical correction. The replication with different ROI sizes (C92) demonstrates robustness. The use of paired t-tests for pre-post comparisons (C96) is appropriate for the within-subjects design.

results.result: ALFF was extracted from ROIs and correlated with connectivity changes using Pearson correlations to assess relationships between local signal changes and remote connectivity modulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C98 describe appropriate methods for relating local signal changes to connectivity changes. The use of Pearson correlations is suitable for this analysis. The method is clearly described and appropriately applied.

results.result: Stochastic DCM was used to assess effective connectivity changes, with bidirectional models between TMS targets and significant clusters, analyzed using paired t-tests at the group level.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C108 describe appropriate DCM methods with proper justification for using stochastic DCM for resting-state data (C102-C103). The model specification (C106) and statistical analysis (C108) are appropriate. Methods are adequately described for the directional connectivity analysis.

results.result: The Kuramoto model with 513 brain regions was used to simulate TMS effects by reducing intrinsic frequency, constrained by structural connectivity from 75 participants, with robustness tested using sparser matrices and distance corrections.
results.evaluation: Claims C109-C122 provide comprehensive description of the computational model with appropriate justification (C110-C112). The use of empirical structural connectivity (C116-C117) and robustness analyses (C119-C121) strengthen the modeling approach. The model choice and implementation are well-justified.

results.result: The model was calibrated to match baseline connectivity (r=0.55 for V1/V2, r=0.45 for FEF) using 500 simulations, with TMS effects simulated by reducing omega across a range of values.
results.evaluation: Claims C123-C132 describe appropriate model calibration and simulation procedures. The correlations between model and data (C128-C129) indicate moderate fit. The systematic exploration of parameter space (C130) and statistical testing (C132) are appropriate. However, the model fits are moderate, suggesting some discrepancy between model and data.

results.result: Background claims establish that the visual system is hierarchically organized with feedforward and feedback connections, with task-dependent modulation and distinct resting-state networks for V1/V2 and FEF.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C54 provide appropriate background context supported by multiple citations to established literature. These claims accurately represent current understanding of visual system organization and set up the rationale for the study.

results.result: Prior work has shown that inhibitory TMS of peripheral nodes can recruit functionally related brain regions, as demonstrated in the sensorimotor system.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C37 accurately cite prior work showing similar effects in other systems, providing context for interpreting the current findings. The citations are appropriate and support the interpretation.

results.result: The work provides novel insights into neural mechanisms underlying effects of local inhibition on large-scale brain dynamics.
results.evaluation: Claim C135 is a summary statement supported by the collective findings showing opposing effects of V1/V2 vs. FEF stimulation and their mechanistic explanation through timescale hierarchies. The novelty claim is justified by the demonstration of site-specific effects and mechanistic modeling.
